However, conservatives living in liberal political climates were less vaccine hesitant than their conservative counterparts living in conservative regions.
Liberals were more likely to receive a booster regardless of political climate, while conservatives’ likelihood was associated with their political climate.
There was a significant interaction between political conservatism and conservative regional climate for vaccine hesitancy, booster hesitancy, and booster status.

The most liberal participants were over 65% likely to get boosted regardless of climate. The most conservative participants in liberal climates were 60% likely to get boosted, while conservatives in conservative climates were less than 35% likely to get boosted (OR =.83, p = .026).
The interaction for vaccination was not significant, this difference between attitudes (hesitancy) and action (vaccination), likely reflects the high prevalence of COVID-19 vaccine mandates.
The present research provides the first assessment of the potential interaction between political orientation, political climate, and COVID vaccination.
This study introduces a novel computational approach to measure subnational and event-driven variation in partisan polarization and explores these dynamics across the United States and Canada.

We demonstrate a strong negative correlation between regional vaccination rates and the degree of polarization in vaccine-related discussions in the U.S., suggesting tangible public health implications of online partisan division.

The cross-national comparison offers particularly valuable insights: while both countries experienced social media polarization, the U.S. showed stronger correlations between polarization, conspiracy theories, and public health outcomes such as vaccination rates.

By tracking the temporal evolution of polarization, we identify distinct spikes linked to specific political events and policy announcements. These polarization surges typically lasted only a few days, revealing the dynamic nature of online partisan discourse.

We collected a large-scale dataset of COVID-19 political discussions on Twitter (now X) occurring between October 9, 2020, to January 4, 2021, comprising approximately 12.5 million tweets linked to the United States and 46.6 million tweets linked to Canada.
We measure polarization by quantifying how far apart the language of left and right-leaning users is positioned in this embedding space, using the C-index, a robust clustering measure.

Automated accounts can contribute disproportionately to partisan discourse by generating large volumes of ideologically slanted content or amplifying existing narratives, potentially inflating the apparent semantic distance between political groups.

Seventh, there are temporal mismatches between our Twitter dataset (collected in late 2020) and regional vaccination rates, which occurred primarily in 2021. The relationship between polarization and public health measures is complex and multidimensional, influenced by numerous social, political, and cultural factors that extend beyond the scope of our computational analysis.

We examine a different possibility. Classical research on political behavior emphasizes that education, internal efficacy, political interest, political knowledge, and participation are central to democratic engagement [17–19]. These factors are often normatively valued because they help citizens follow politics and take part in democratic life. Yet even classical theories recognized that engagement could become excessive [20], and more recent work on motivated reasoning and political polarization suggests that politically engaged citizens may also be more likely to process information in biased or antagonistic ways [21]. We extend this revisionist perspective to online political hostility by asking whether hostile political expression on X/Twitter is associated not only with deprivation or personality-based explanations, but also with political engagement and its antecedents.
Online political hostility is positively associated with these indicators, with the strongest associations for political interest, political knowledge, and online participation.

The associations between online political hostility and indicators of political engagement and its antecedents are more pronounced for some indicators, especially online and offline participation, among users with more polarized affect directed towards US political leaders.

We therefore turn to our exploratory expectation and examine whether users who express more online political hostility are also more active on X/Twitter and have greater potential reach. These analyses are exploratory and descriptive. We investigate the visibility of politically hostile users by first showing results from count models that examine whether those who are politically hostile (a) post more, (b) have more friends, and (c) have more followers.

We rely on a data infrastructure combining panel survey data with online behavioral data from X (see also [59]). To obtain our data, we commissioned the survey agency YouGov to invite panelists from their standing web panel to participate in a series of panel surveys. We recruited the original set of panelists in January 2019. Here, participants were asked to complete a survey with measures of our set of potential antecedents of online political hostility and, importantly, to provide their X ID and give consent to let us scrape their publicly available X data and link it to their survey answers.

Our key measure of online political hostility is based on a word embeddings approach termed the Super-Unsupervised (SU) approach [60]. The gist of the method is that through their use of language in posts, respondents themselves define what constitutes the linguistic space of political hostility.

Face validity of the overall measure. To assess the face validity of the overall measure [60], inspected the posts with the highest and lowest political hostility scores. The posts with the highest scores clearly contained hostile language directed at political out-groups (e.g., derogatory characterizations of political opponents, calls for violence against political groups, and moralized criticism). In contrast, the posts with the lowest scores were either neutral or positive in tone and did not contain any hostile language.
All models control for the Big Five personality traits, income, age, gender, and party identification.

For the panel analyses, we use Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models (RI-CLPM). These models separate stable between-person differences from within-person change and therefore reduce concerns that the associations are entirely driven by stable time-invariant characteristics such as long-standing socioeconomic factors or broad personality traits.

The associations were obtained after controlling for broad personality traits, income, age, gender, and party identification. The largest associations are generally observed for the primary measure of political hostility rather than for the more general AFINN or Perspective API measures.

Fig 4 displays the associations separately for users above and below the midpoint of the leader-directed affective-polarization scale. The descriptive pattern suggests that the association between engagement and hostility is often stronger among more affectively polarized users.

A change from the mean level of hostility to 1.5 standard deviations above the mean is associated with an increase in the number of posts from around 420 to around 900 and an increase in the number of followers from around 220 to around 370.

This pattern is consistent with recent research on motivated reasoning, partisan animus, and the darker sides of political engagement [21,33,47,82]. In a polarized political context, politically engaged citizens may be more likely to enter conflictual political exchanges, and affective polarization may make those exchanges more antagonistic.

However, the moderation evidence is not uniform across all indicators. Formal interaction models (Fig 3) show the clearest support for online and offline participation, while the evidence is weaker or inconsistent for more distal antecedents such as education.

First, the data come from American X/Twitter users. This platform is a public, text-based, and highly political platform, and the associations observed here may not generalize directly to platforms with different affordances, audiences, moderation systems, or norms of interaction.

The findings should overall be interpreted as associational rather than causal. Political sophistication or partisan involvement may be common causes of both participation and hostility. Affective polarization may increase engagement, engagement may increase affective polarization, and hostile online interaction may itself intensify affective polarization.

The survey did not include measures of those more specific traits, and we therefore cannot adjudicate those accounts directly. Instead, the Big Five controls help assess whether the associations remain after accounting for broad personality differences.
We therefore interpret the moderation analyses as evidence about leader-directed affective polarization and discuss this measurement limitation below.
We therefore interpret the SU score as an aggregate indicator of online political hostility and assess the robustness of the findings using additional measures.

Recent research has more strongly emphasized this revisionist view on the costs and benefits of political engagement. Most clearly, the literature on political information processing has argued and found that indicators of political engagement (e.g., partisanship) can be associated with biased assessments of political arguments and news such that arguments and news that are aligned with an individual’s political opinions are evaluated less critically by the engaged than arguments and news that are not aligned [21,47].

In the realm of adolescent social network research, the correlation between substance use and friendship formation is well-documented. Non-AI researchers have used the recurring connection between substance use and friendship formation as a basis for intervention research with promising results [47]. Our study’s finding that substance use is not associated with relational patterns among 9th and 10th-grade AI youth marks a significant departure from established trends, offering a novel perspective. This finding not only underscores a fundamental lack of theoretical understanding regarding developmental relationship patterns within this demographic but also signals the urgent need to explore more deeply the factors influencing relational dynamics among AI youth.
These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.

Using exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties. Models assessed endogenous structural processes (reciprocity, transitivity, degree effects) and actor-level characteristics, including demographic factors, substance use (alcohol, tobacco, marijuana), depression, and AI identity.

Trained research team members administered the survey during school hours. Students provided responses directly on tablets. Written informed assent was obtained digitally from all participants, with hard copies provided afterward.

The survey also included a measure of depression, utilizing the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) [35–38]. This section of the survey consisted of six questions, each probing different facets of depression... The measurement of AI identity was assessed using six items adapted from the Affirmation and Belonging subscale of the Multigroup Ethnic Identity Measure (MEIM) [39].

The ERGM results revealed strong and consistent endogenous structural effects across all three schools (Table 3). Reciprocity was positive and highly significant in every model, indicating a robust tendency for mutual friendship nominations. Similarly, the positive coefficients for closed triads (transitivity) and negative coefficients for two‑path confirmed that triadic closure—the process by which friends of friends become friends—is a fundamental organizing principle within these AI adolescent networks.

Homophily effects provided further evidence of distinct relational logics. Gender and grade homophily were consistently significant across all schools (AME = 0.008–0.058, all p < 0.001), indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation.

Substance use demonstrated no consistent or robust association with friendship dynamics in this sample. Sender and receiver effects—indicating whether individuals who use substances are more likely to receive or initiate friendships—were almost entirely non-significant across all three schools and substances.

Depression sender and receiver effects were substantively negligible across all schools; although the sender effect in School B reached statistical significance across model specifications owing to very small standard errors, its magnitude (AME < 0.001) indicates no meaningful association, and AI identity was largely unassociated with sending or receiving ties, with only a borderline positive receiver effect in School C.

AI identity homophily was consistently non-significant across all schools. This null finding, while seemingly counterintuitive given the cultural emphasis on tribal belonging, is consistent with several contextual considerations. First, in AI-majority schools, racial identity is a near-universal attribute; with nearly all students identifying as AI, there is insufficient variation in racial category for identity to differentiate friendship choices.
Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics.

The cross-sectional design imposes a fundamental interpretive limit: a single, simultaneous observation of the network and of individual attributes cannot capture changes in network formation and behavior over time. More importantly, cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time [4,18,48].
Third, kinship networks and familial relationships—which operate largely outside the school-based friendship system we measured—may be the primary arena where AI identity shapes social ties [27].

This study examines the structural and relational foundations of friendship networks among AI adolescents in their unique cultural context. Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties.

One study that did focus specifically on AI youth network characteristics is Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17], who used Add Health to describe AI networks in heterogeneous school contexts, finding that AI adolescents had fewer reciprocated friendships than White peers. However, their analysis was primarily descriptive and did not model the endogenous network processes examined here.
